name: Somerset Redstreak

origin.parentage: Unknown; not the same as the seventeenth-century Herefordshire Redstreak

history: A Somerset bittersweet of the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, unrelated except in name to the famous old Herefordshire Redstreak. It gained a modern profile through single-variety commercial ciders.

look.description: Attractive rounded fruit, bright red stripes over yellow, tough-skinned with a little russet.

taste.summary: A mild-to-medium bittersweet; the greenish-white flesh is sweet and juicy but rubbery and astringent to bite. Its juice gives a soft, fruity cider.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill Oct, within two or three weeks of picking.

tree.notes: Vigorous, fairly upright tree reported to yield very well.

grow_notes: An early bittersweet, useful for starting the pressing season. Give its vigorous upright growth room on a standard or half-standard.

name: Médaille d'Or
history: First propagated around 1865 by the nurseryman Godard at Bois-Guillaume outside Rouen, it won a gold medal from the Seine-Inférieure horticultural society in 1873, hence the name. It reached England in the 1880s.

look.description: Small golden-yellow apple marbled with fine brown russet, often heavier on the sunny side.

taste.summary: A full bittersweet with exceptionally high sugar and tannin and little acid; the juice is rich and aromatic but intensely astringent, so it is usually blended.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, spreading tree; productive but tends to crop in alternate years.

pollination.notes: Very late flowering; choose an equally late pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mild Atlantic climates like Normandy and western England, with long autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season areas where its very late fruit cannot ripen.

health.other: Some scab resistance; some fire blight susceptibility; biennial.

grow_notes: Use sparingly in blends for sugar and tannin. Plant with other very late bloomers such as Dabinett or Stoke Red. Its late blossom avoids most spring frosts.

name: Porter's Perfection
history: Associated with Charles Porter of East Lambrook in south Somerset and introduced in the early 1900s. A late bittersharp valued for blending and occasionally for single-variety cider.

look.description: Conical fruit with a pale cream ground mostly covered by a dark red flush.

taste.summary: A bittersharp with high acid and fairly mild tannin; tart if picked early or grown in a cool spot, it needs a few weeks of storage before milling.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; store about a month, then mill Dec.

tree.notes: Vigorous, heavy-cropping tree with some tendency to alternate years.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates with long autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season regions; the very late fruit needs a long autumn.

health.other: Generally healthy, with some resistance to scab and canker.

grow_notes: One of the last cider apples to pick; let the fruit mellow in store before pressing. A good source of acid to balance bittersweets.

name: Major

origin.place: South Devon and the Blackdown Hills, Somerset, England

history: A long-established bittersweet of nineteenth-century or earlier date, found in old farm orchards across South Devon and on the eastern side of the Blackdown Hills. Rated as of vintage quality.

look.description: Medium, typical 'Jersey'-type fruit with a pinkish-red flush.

taste.summary: A full bittersweet: high tannin, low acid and good sugar, giving a well-structured cider that can stand alone.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill late Sep-Oct.

tree.notes: Triploid; young trees grow very vigorously, so it is unsuited to the most vigorous rootstocks.

pollination.notes: Triploid, so a poor pollen donor; plant with two other compatible varieties.

grow_notes: Use a moderate rootstock to tame its vigour. As an early bittersweet it pairs with early sharps for the first pressings. Remember it needs two pollinators as a triploid.

name: Sweet Alford
history: A Devon cider apple reputed to date from the eighteenth century, grown as a high-quality sweet. Rated a vintage variety capable of single-variety cider.

look.description: Small, flattened-conical apple with waxy pale yellow skin, a pink flush and russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Sweet, juicy, fairly crisp white flesh with only a faint astringency; the juice is sweet and makes a soft, mild bittersweet-leaning cider that balances sharper fruit.

tree.notes: Little published information on tree habit.

pollination.notes: Reported to blossom in mid spring; group not reliably recorded.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp South West England; also grown in North American and New Zealand cider collections.

grow_notes: Grow it to sweeten and soften blends built on bittersharps. Plant with another mid-season flowering cider variety.
